**Before the visit**
- Add the visit date on the Visit tab. MenoMap shows how complete your notes are and what would make them stronger.
- Choose the most important topics and questions. Narrow them to three or four.
- Create notes from the last 30 or 90 days. Check that your medication list is up to date.

**At the visit**
- Hand over or show the first page. It is made to be read in under a minute: counts, averages, the heat calendar and your questions.
- Start with the question that matters most to you.
- If your doctor speaks another language, you can create the notes in that language.

**What the notes are and what they are not**

They are a summary of what you have logged, plus data you chose to bring in from the Health app. They are not a diagnosis nor a complete medical record, and the patterns shown in them are coincidence checks, not proof of a cause. Your doctor may ask things the notes do not answer, and that is normal.

**After the visit**

Add any new medication and its start date. After a few weeks MenoMap can show your entries before and after, which makes the next assessment easier.
backTranslations.42:
**Menopause** is a single point in time: the day when 12 months in a row have passed without a period, when it is not explained by another cause (such as pregnancy, certain medications or surgery). In many countries it falls on average a little over age 50, but any age between about 45 and 55 is common.

**Perimenopause** is the period of years before it. Hormone levels rise and fall unevenly, so periods can become irregular, heavier or lighter, and come more or less often. Many changes associated with the change of life, such as hot flashes, night sweats, sleep changes and mood changes, often begin already at this stage, while periods still come. Perimenopause can last a few years or clearly longer, and it is different for everyone.

**Postmenopause** is everything after that 12-month mark. Some symptoms settle over time, others can continue for years.

Menopause can also come earlier because of surgery that removes the ovaries, some cancer treatments or other conditions. Menopause that comes before age 40 is sometimes called premature ovarian insufficiency, and it is worth discussing with a doctor.

**How it is recognised.** In many people over 45, a doctor recognises perimenopause or menopause from the history and symptoms. Blood tests are not always needed, because hormone levels fluctuate from day to day. They are more likely to be used if the person is younger or the situation is unclear.

**What MenoMap does and does not do.** MenoMap cannot tell what stage you are in. It can, however, keep an honest record of what you notice: waves (hot flashes), sleep, mood and treatment, so that you and your doctor can look at the same overall picture.

backTranslations.162:
Doctors call hot flashes and night sweats **vasomotor symptoms**. A hot flash is a sudden feeling of heat, often on the face, neck and chest, sometimes with flushing, sweating, a fast heartbeat or chills afterwards. A night sweat is the same thing during sleep, and it can be so strong that it wakes you or soaks the sheets.

They are the most common changes of the change of life. Some have a few mild ones, others many in a day, and they disturb work and sleep. For some they fade within a few years, for others they last much longer.

**What can make them more likely.** Many notice links with alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, hot rooms, stress or thick bedding. These vary a lot from person to person, which is why tracking your own tags can be more useful than a general list.

**There are other causes too.** Flushing and sweating can also be caused by thyroid problems, infections, some medications, anxiety and other conditions. If your symptoms do not fit the usual picture or are accompanied by weight loss, fever or feeling unwell, tell your doctor.

**Describe them well.** Useful information at the visit:
- How many in the day and at night, roughly
- How strong they feel and how long they last
- What they interrupt: sleep, work, conversations, exercise
- What they seem to be preceded by
- What you have tried and whether it changed anything

MenoMap's Wave button and after-the-fact logging are made to capture exactly this without much effort.

**Help is available.** There are hormonal and non-hormonal treatment options and practical measures. Which of them suit you is something worth discussing with a doctor.

backTranslations.291:
Hormone therapy (also called hormone replacement therapy, HRT or MHT) replaces part of the estrogen that the body produces less of around the time of the change of life. According to key treatment guidelines, it is an effective treatment for many for hot flashes and night sweats, and it can also help with other symptoms.

**It comes in different forms:** as patches, gels, sprays, tablets, and as low-dose vaginal preparations for local symptoms such as dryness. For those who still have a uterus, a progestogen (corpus luteum hormone) is usually prescribed alongside the estrogen to protect the lining of the uterus.

**Benefits and risks depend on the person:** age, how long it has been since periods ended, your own and family medical history (for example breast cancer, blood clots, stroke or heart disease), and the type and route of treatment. That is why it is decided together with a doctor who knows your history, and it is not something an app can decide.

**Frequently asked:**
- Is hormone therapy an option for me, and why or why not?
- What type and form would you recommend, and why?
- What benefits could I expect, and how soon?
- What are my personal risks, and how do they compare to not being treated?
- What should I monitor, and when will the treatment be re-evaluated?

**If you already use it,** log it in MenoMap (You → Medications). MenoMap shows your waves before and after starting the treatment as a coincidence check, not proof, so you have something concrete to discuss at a follow-up visit.

MenoMap never suggests starting, stopping or changing a medication.

backTranslations.293:
Hormone therapy is not suitable for everyone, and some simply want to try other approaches. There are several.

**Prescription medications.** For some non-hormonal medications there is evidence of effectiveness in reducing hot flashes. These include certain medications originally developed for other conditions and a newer class of medication developed specifically for hot flashes. Each has its own benefits, side effects and interactions, so a doctor can help you weigh them.

**Talking therapies and mind–body methods.** For cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) adapted to the change of life there is evidence that it reduces the bother of hot flashes and night sweats and improves sleep. Clinical hypnosis has also been studied.

**Practical changes many benefit from:**
- Layers of clothing that come off quickly
- A fan on the desk and beside the bed
- A cooler bedroom and breathable bedding
- Noticing and reducing your own triggers (MenoMap's tags and experiments help with this)
- Regular exercise and a regular sleep rhythm

**Supplements and herbal products.** For many of them the evidence of effectiveness is conflicting or scant, quality varies, and some have interactions with other medications. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about everything you use, including products available without a prescription.

**Try one change at a time.** MenoMap's two-week experiments compare your own entries before the change and during it, which is easier to evaluate than a mere feeling.

backTranslations.416:
Most appointments are short, and a month of nights is hard to remember in the moment. What stays in mind is usually the most recent or worst days. Simple record-keeping fills the gap.

**What a diary tells your doctor:**
- How often symptoms occur and how strong they are, not just that they exist
- Whether things are improving, getting worse or staying the same
- What happened around them: sleep, alcohol, stress, medications
- A baseline to compare against if you try a treatment

**Keep it light.** A diary is only useful if you keep it. MenoMap is built around a one-tap Wave button and a four-question evening survey, so it takes seconds, not a notebook.

**Two weeks is a good start.** Entries over two to four weeks usually give a clearer picture than one bad week.

**Bring your questions too.** Write down what matters most to you: the most bothersome symptom, what you want to try or avoid, and anything that worries you. MenoMap's Visit tab helps choose the questions and prints them with your notes.

backTranslations.479:
When you have not had a period for 12 months, **any vaginal bleeding must be examined by a doctor**, even if it has happened only once and even if it was only spotting or a pink or brown discharge.

Most often the cause turns out to be harmless. For example, thinning of the vagina or the uterine lining is common. However, bleeding after menopause can sometimes be an early sign of a condition that is much easier to treat when found early. That is why health authority guidance advises having it examined rather than waiting.

**If you use hormone therapy,** a certain kind of bleeding may be expected depending on the type of treatment. Bleeding that is unexpected for your treatment, heavier than usual, or comes at the wrong time must also be examined.

**What to do:**
- Contact your doctor or health services and say that you have had bleeding after menopause.
- Note the date, the amount of bleeding and anything else you noticed. MenoMap can keep this information for you (You → Menstrual cycle).

MenoMap cannot tell why the bleeding occurred. It reminds you to have it examined and includes it in your visit notes.

backTranslations.529:
Poor sleep is one of the most common complaints of midlife, and it rarely has just one cause.

**Night sweats** can wake you directly or leave you so hot or damp that it is hard to fall asleep again.

**Other common factors:**
- Needing to urinate at night
- Anxiety or racing thoughts
- Alcohol, which can help you fall asleep but often disrupts the latter half of the night
- Caffeine late in the day
- Pain, restless legs or a partner's snoring
- Snoring or breathing pauses, which can be a sign of sleep apnea (worth bringing up, especially if you are very sleepy during the day)

**What usually helps people.** A cool, dark room; breathable bedding and layers you can take off; a regular wake-up time; and less alcohol near bedtime. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured and well-studied method, and many doctors can refer you to it.

**What to track.** For a week or two log your sleep score, night waves, alcohol and late caffeine. MenoMap's evening survey and wave log handle this with a few taps. If you use an Apple Watch, MenoMap can show the Health app's sleep and wrist temperature data alongside your night sweats as background, not as an explanation.

**When to seek examination.** Talk to a doctor if poor sleep affects your safety (for example when driving), your mood or your daily life, or if you notice breathing pauses or gasping at night.
